content: 1. The effectiveness of the home safety assessment and modification program appeared to be reduced when individuals were also participating in an exercise program. This observation raises questions about whether the reduction in falls was attributable to the occupational therapist's visit or the home modifications themselves. 2. A systematic review on home injuries for the WHO Housing and Health Guidelines included a study by Pressley (2005) that analyzed cross-sectional data from individuals aged 18 years and younger discharged from U.S. hospitals. The study excluded individuals aged 19 years or older and routine or elective admissions for falls from buildings or structures, as these were unlikely to represent incident injuries. 3. The Pressley study utilized data from the Kids Inpatient Database (KID-HCUP), which provided a national sample of acute care hospital discharges from 27 U.S. states. The analysis included 2,163,402 individuals aged 18 years and younger discharged in the year 2000. The study examined the impact of legislation-based window fall prevention programs, such as window guards, in areas with and without such legislation. 4. Limitations of the Pressley study included the inclusion of non-window-related falls from buildings (e.g., fire escapes) and the lack of data on individuals who died before hospital admission, did not seek treatment, or were treated and released from emergency departments. 5. Kendrick (2005) conducted a cohort study in the United Kingdom investigating the relationship between child, family, and neighborhood characteristics and childhood injuries. The study focused on children under 5 years old and was nested within the control arm of a randomized trial evaluating the effectiveness of health visitor interventions and access to free or low-cost safety equipment. 6. The Kendrick study had a robust methodology, sufficient statistical power, and high follow-up rates. However, it did not report participation rates for cases and controls, and it was unclear whether a history of previous home injuries was considered when selecting controls. 7. LeBlanc (2006) conducted a multicenter case-control study in Canada examining the association between home safety measures and the risk of unintentional injuries among children under 8 years old. Cases included children presenting to emergency departments for falls, scalds, burns, poisoning, ingestion, or choking at home, while controls were ageand sex-matched children presenting with non-injury-related diagnoses. 8. The LeBlanc study included 692 participants (346 cases and 346 controls) but did not report participation rates. Controls were matched only for age and sex, and it was unclear if prior home injury history was accounted for. The study also reported other exposures not relevant to the systematic review. 9. Keall (2008) conducted a retrospective cohort study in New Zealand examining the association between the number of home injury hazards and home injuries. The study included 102 households with 255 members and assessed hazards such as slippery bathroom floors, unsafe electrical wiring, and poorly lit stairs. 10. Injury outcomes in the Keall study were assessed using data from the New Zealand Accident Compensation Corporation, which records injuries requiring medical intervention. Limitations included a small sample size, low cooperation rate, and temporal ambiguity due to the retrospective design. 11. Fitzharris (2010) conducted the Whitehorse No Falls Trial, a randomized trial in Australia with a factorial design. The study included 1,090 participants aged 70 and above and evaluated interventions such as exercise, home hazard modification (HHM), and vision correction, both individually and in combination. 12. The Fitzharris study demonstrated adequate randomization and allocation concealment but could not blind participants due to the nature of the interventions. The study found that HHM reduced falls requiring medical care, but the combined intervention analyses adjusted for the effects of other interventions. 13. Leclerc (2010) conducted a cohort study in Canada examining the relationship between home hazards and falls among community-dwelling seniors receiving home-care services. The study used a 37-item checklist to assess multiple exposures, including lighting and furniture, but only some exposures were relevant to the systematic review. 14. Limitations of the Leclerc study included the use of convenience sampling, self-reported outcome assessment via telephone questionnaires, and the inability to differentiate between exposures of interest and other exposures. 15. Mashreky (2010) conducted a nested case-control study in rural Bangladesh investigating determinants of childhood burns. Cases included children under 10 years old who sustained burns within the previous year, while controls were age-, sex-, and socioeconomic status-matched children with no burn history. 16. The Mashreky study included 840 participants (420 cases and 420 controls) and identified risk factors such as unprotected hot surfaces. Limitations included inadequate comparison of cases and controls, reliance on face-to-face interviews for exposure measurement, and limited adjustment for potential confounders. 17. Phelan (2011) conducted a randomized controlled trial in the U.S. evaluating the effectiveness of home injury hazard reduction interventions among mothers and their children under 3 years old. The intervention included home assessments and modifications such as stair gates, cabinet locks, and smoke detectors. 18. The Phelan study included 355 participants (181 intervention, 174 control) and assessed medically attended injuries, including falls, cuts, and burns. Randomization was computer-generated, and investigators were masked until the end of data analysis. Limitations included the inability to mask participants and reliance on self-reported outcomes. 19. Taira (2011) conducted a case-control study in the U.S. examining predictors of burn injuries. Cases included burn patients from a burn registry, while controls were non-burned emergency department attendees. The study found higher rates of safe storage of flammable liquids among cases but noted that the non-random nature of the control group was a key limitation. 20. Pearce (2012) analyzed data from the UK Millennium Cohort Study to investigate the influence of the home environment on inequalities in unintentional injuries among children aged 9 months to 3 years. The study included 18,296 singleton children born in the UK between September 2000 and January 2002.
